cells.tense: You're here, right now, tending something that's still growing, and it isn't wearing you out.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've grown that's close to ready and let it stand on its own — not dropped, finished. What comes back is care that costs less than it gives, and a hold that doesn't tighten.
cells.core:
You're here, right now, tending something that's still growing, and it isn't wearing you out. You can carry weight and stay gentle with what's under it at the same time — you're not gripping it to keep it alive and you're not bracing to keep it from leaving. It's growing because you're steady, not because you're pushing. That's the kind of holding that lasts.

So here's what this is free to feed next: pick one thing you've grown that's close to ready and let it stand on its own. Not dropped — finished. Letting go of something because it's done is the last act of caring for it, and it hands you back the room to carry what's actually still young.
cells.sheetLine: You hold what's growing steadily, without squeezing it.

cells.tense: You're already living in the future where they can't do this without you, and you're arranging the present to prove it.
cells.ask: Take one step toward what you're caring for without knowing how it turns out — enough light for that step, none for the road. What comes back is a hold that stays steady without closing.
cells.core:
You're already living in the future where they can't do this without you, and you're arranging the present to prove it. The care is real, and it's gone past tending into managing — you're carrying what's growing so tightly that it has no room left to grow on its own, and the strength you have for holding is being spent on steering. Where you end and the thing you're caring for begins has gotten hard to find, and that blur is what's tiring you.

The way back isn't less care. It's less certainty. Take one step toward what you're caring for without knowing how it turns out — enough light for that step, none for the road. Not knowing isn't a failure of care; it's the condition growth happens in. A hold that can stay steady without closing is the one that lets something become what it is.
cells.sheetLine: You're protecting it so hard it can't grow.

cells.tense: Somewhere behind you, caring for something that was growing cost more than you could carry, and you're still paying by not starting anything new.
cells.ask: Don't go back to tending yet — name one thing you'd actually want to see grow, and let the wanting lead. What comes back is care that doesn't drain you, because it's pulling toward something instead of pushing against nothing.
cells.core:
Somewhere behind you, caring for something that was growing cost more than you could carry, and you're still paying by not starting anything new. Nothing's taking root — not because you can't hold weight, you plainly can, but because you've stopped putting anything soft in your hands. It reads as self-sufficient from the outside. From the inside it's a field left fallow long enough that you've forgotten you're the one who left it.

Don't go back to tending yet; the ground is empty and effort poured straight into empty ground just drains. Go to the other end of it instead: name one thing you'd actually want to see grow. Just the wanting — what you'd be glad to look up and find alive. Let that pull the care back out of you, rather than trying to shove it back in. Care that's drawn toward something doesn't exhaust the way care forced against nothing does.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped growing anything, and called it independence.

cells.tense: You're the one everyone's leaning on right now, and you'd say you just ended up here.
cells.ask: Set down one thing you've been carrying that nobody actually handed you, and say — to yourself, once — "I'm done with this one." What comes back is a hold that's chosen, which is the only kind that doesn't tighten.
cells.core:
You're the one everyone's leaning on right now, and you'd say you just ended up here. Other people experience you as the one who tends — the steady one, the one who can take it — and you experience the weight without the credit, because you never signed on to any of it. The caring is running, all of it, in your hands. The choosing got left out, and that's what's leaving you empty.

The way back is smaller than you'd think. Set down one thing you've been carrying that nobody actually handed you, and say — to yourself, once — "I'm done with this one." Not because it failed; because it's complete, or it was never yours to grow. Choosing what to release is how you find out the rest was chosen too. A hold you've claimed is the only kind that doesn't tighten.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying what everyone's growing, and calling it an accident.
